a2-present-continuous.title: Present Continuous (-Iyor)
a2-present-continuous.explanation: Turkish forms the present continuous by attaching -Iyor to the verb stem, with the connecting vowel following 4-way vowel harmony (ı/i/u/ü) based on the stem's last vowel. If the stem ends in a vowel, that vowel drops before -Iyor is added. This tense covers both actions happening right now and, very commonly in everyday speech, habitual actions -- 'Her sabah erken kalkıyorum' (I get up early every morning) is completely natural, not just 'I am getting up' in the moment.
a2-present-continuous.fact: Unlike the aorist (-Ir) tense, -Iyor attaches the same way to every verb with zero irregular exceptions -- once you know the harmony rule, you can conjugate any verb in this tense correctly.

dialogue.en: What are you doing right now?
I'm having breakfast.

a2-past-di.title: Definite Past (-DI)
a2-past-di.pattern: stem + -DI (harmonized: dı/di/du/dü or tı/ti/tu/tü) + personal ending
a2-past-di.explanation: The -DI suffix marks events the speaker witnessed or is certain happened -- Turkey's everyday 'I did X' past tense. Its vowel follows 4-way harmony (dı/di/du/dü) based on the stem's last vowel, and the consonant becomes t instead of d if the stem ends in a voiceless consonant (p, ç, t, k, f, s, ş, h) -- so gitmek gives gittim (t stays t), but gelmek gives geldim (l is voiced, so d stays d).
a2-past-di.fact: -DI is one of the most reliably regular suffixes in Turkish -- once you know the harmony and devoicing rules, the only real irregularity in this whole tense is a small set of verbs whose STEM itself changes (like gitmek's git-/gid- alternation, which shows up in other tenses, not this one).

dialogue.en: What did you do yesterday?
I went to the movies with my friends.

a2-past-mis.title: Reported Past (-mIş)
a2-past-mis.explanation: -mIş marks things the speaker did NOT personally witness: hearsay, rumor, things learned secondhand, or things discovered/realized after the fact. It contrasts directly with -DI, which marks events the speaker is certain about or saw happen. Its vowel follows the same 4-way harmony as -DI (mış/miş/muş/müş), but since the suffix starts with the consonant m rather than d, there's no devoicing rule to worry about -- it attaches the same way after every stem.
a2-past-mis.fact: -mIş also attaches to nouns and adjectives (with a y buffer after a vowel) to report a STATE secondhand -- 'yorgunmuş' (apparently tired), 'pahalıymış' (apparently expensive) -- not just verbs.

dialogue.tr: Duydun mu, yeni bir kafe açılmış.
dialogue.en: Did you hear, a new cafe has apparently opened.
No, I hadn't heard, let's go check it out.

a2-future.title: Future Tense (-EcEk)
a2-future.explanation: The future suffix -EcEk has only 2-way harmony (ecek after front vowels, acak after back vowels) rather than the 4-way harmony of -Iyor/-DI/-mIş. A y-buffer is inserted if the stem ends in a vowel. Its own final k softens to ğ whenever a vowel-initial personal ending follows (1st person singular -im and 1st person plural -iz), which is why 'gitmek' gives 'gideceğim' (I will go) but plain 'gidecek' (he/she will go, no personal ending after it).
a2-future.fact: Like -Iyor, the intervocalic softening that turns git- into gid- also happens here (gid-ecek), since -EcEk starts with a vowel -- but most verbs' stem-final consonant does NOT soften this way; git-/gid- and et-/ed- are the two everyday verbs where you'll see it constantly.

dialogue.en: What will you do this weekend?
I will go to the movies with my friends.

a2-possessive.title: Possessive Suffixes
a2-possessive.explanation: Turkish marks 'my/your/his/our/your(pl)/their X' with a suffix on the noun itself, not a separate possessive word: ev (house) -> evim (my house), evin (your house), evi (his/her house). Consonant-final stems take -Im/-In/-I directly (4-way harmony); vowel-final stems take -m/-n/-sI, with an s-buffer for the 3rd person form so two vowels don't collide (araba -> arabası, not 'arabaı').
a2-possessive.fact: The same p/ç/t/k softening seen in verbs also happens to nouns before a vowel-initial possessive suffix -- kitap (book) becomes kitabım (my book), not 'kitapım'.

dialogue.en: Is this your book?
Yes, it's my book.

a2-cases.title: The Four Cases (Accusative, Dative, Locative, Ablative)
a2-cases.explanation: Turkish marks a noun's grammatical role with a case suffix instead of word order or a preposition: eve (to home), evde (at home), evden (from home), evi (the house, as a definite object). Accusative and dative have y-buffers after vowel-final stems and full 4-way (accusative) or 2-way (dative) harmony; locative and ablative both start with D, which devoices to T after a voiceless-final stem (parkta, not 'parkda'). Only DEFINITE direct objects take the accusative -- 'bir ceket almak istiyorum' (I want to buy a jacket, indefinite, no suffix) vs. 'bu ceketi alıyorum' (I'm buying this jacket, definite, -i attached).
a2-cases.fact: When a case suffix attaches after a 3rd-person possessive ending (-I/-sI), an extra -n- buffer appears: ev-i (his house) but ev-i-nde (in his house), ev-i-nden (from his house) -- a leftover of Turkish's historical grammar that's now just a fixed rule to memorize.

dialogue.en: Where are you going?
I'm going home, I'm very tired.

a2-postpositions.title: Postpositions and Connectors
a2-postpositions.explanation: Turkish postpositions come AFTER the noun they govern, the mirror image of an English preposition: 'senin için' (for you), 'benim gibi' (like me). 'İle' (with) is so common it's usually fused onto the noun as a suffix instead: arkadaşım + ile -> arkadaşımla. 'Önce' (before) and 'sonra' (after) pair with the ablative case: yemekten önce (before eating), yemekten sonra (after eating).
a2-postpositions.fact: The negative aorist (-mAz/-mEz, used in fixed phrases like 'fark etmez' -- it doesn't matter) is fully regular for every verb, even the handful of verbs whose POSITIVE aorist is irregular (etmek's positive is 'eder', but its negative is still the expected 'etmez').

dialogue.en: Why are you learning Turkish?
Because I love Turkey a lot.

a2-comparison.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
a2-comparison.pattern: X-den daha Y (more Y than X); en Y (the most Y); X Z kadar Y (as Y as Z)
a2-comparison.explanation: Turkish comparison doesn't change the adjective itself the way English '-er/-est' does -- it uses separate words. 'Daha' (more) goes before the adjective, and what you're comparing against takes the ablative case: 'Ali Ahmet'ten daha çalışkan' (Ali is more hardworking than Ahmet, literally 'from Ahmet'). 'En' (most) simply goes before the adjective for a superlative, with no case needed since there's nothing being compared against.
a2-comparison.fact: The same p/ç/t/k softening from nouns and verbs applies to adjectives too when a vowel-initial personal suffix follows: küçük (small) + üm (I am) becomes küçüğüm, not 'küçüküm'.

dialogue.en: Which house is bigger?

dialogue.tr: Bu ev o evden daha büyük.
dialogue.en: This house is bigger than that house.

a2-obligation.title: Obligation (-mAlI)
a2-obligation.explanation: -mAlI expresses 'must/should', with only 2-way harmony (malı after back vowels, meli after front vowels) and no buffer consonants or irregular exceptions to worry about -- it attaches to every verb stem the same simple way. The negative 'shouldn't' inserts -mA- before it: unut-ma-malı-yım (I shouldn't forget).
a2-obligation.fact: Unlike -Iyor and -EcEk, -mAlI never triggers the git-/gid- or et-/ed- style stem-consonant softening, because it starts with a consonant (m) -- gitmeliyim (I must go), not 'gidmeliyim'.

dialogue.en: What must I do today?
First you should go to the doctor.

b1-relative-en.title: Relative Clauses with -En
b1-relative-en.explanation: Turkish builds 'the person/thing who/that does X' by turning the verb into an adjective with -En, placed BEFORE the noun it describes -- the mirror image of English word order. 'Koşan adam' is literally 'running man' = 'the man who is running/runs'. -En only has 2-way harmony (en after front vowels, an after back vowels), with a y-buffer after vowel-final stems, and it's used specifically when the SUBJECT of the relative clause is what's being described (the man WHO runs, not the man someone else saw running).
b1-relative-en.fact: -En starts with a vowel, so it triggers the same git-/gid- style softening as -Iyor and -EcEk: gitmek (to go) gives 'giden' (the one who goes/is going), not 'giten'.

dialogue.en: Who opened the door?
I don't know, I wasn't the one who opened it.

b1-relative-dik.title: Relative Clauses with -DIk
b1-relative-dik.pattern: verb stem + -DIk (harmonized: dık/dik/duk/dük, devoiced to tık/tik/tuk/tük after voiceless stems) + possessive + noun
b1-relative-dik.explanation: -DIk is the other half of Turkish relative clauses, used when the described noun is the OBJECT of the action (or when the doer needs to be specified) rather than the subject: 'okuduğum kitap' (the book I read) vs. -En's 'okuyan kişi' (the person who reads). A possessive suffix on -DIk marks WHO did the action -- oku-duk-um (my having-read) kitap, oku-duk-un (your having-read) kitap, oku-duk-u (his/her having-read) kitap.
b1-relative-dik.fact: -DIk's own final k softens to ğ before the vowel-initial possessive suffixes (-um, -un, -umuz, -unuz), same p/ç/t/k pattern seen everywhere else: gördüğüm (the thing I saw), not 'gördüküm'.

dialogue.en: How was the book you read yesterday?
The book I read was very good.

b1-ability.title: Ability (-Ebil)
b1-ability.pattern: stem + -(y)Ebil (harmonized: ebil/abil) + tense; negative: stem + -(y)EmE + tense
b1-ability.explanation: 'Can/be able to' is built by inserting -Ebil right after the verb stem, then adding a normal tense suffix: gid-ebil-di-m (I was able to go, past), gid-ebil-eceğim (I will be able to go, future), gid-ebil-iyorum (I can go, present continuous -- very common in everyday speech for general ability, not just an action in progress). The negative uses a DIFFERENT infix, -(y)EmE- instead of -Ebil-: gid-eme-dim (I couldn't go), gid-emi-yorum (I can't go).
b1-ability.fact: The habitual/general 'can' also has an aorist form (gidebilirim), but -Ebiliyor (present continuous) covers the same everyday meaning just as naturally and is extremely common in casual speech -- so you'll hear both.

dialogue.en: Can you speak Turkish?
I can speak a little, I'm still learning.

b1-gerekmek.title: Necessity with gerekmek
b1-gerekmek.explanation: Besides -mAlI, Turkish has a second, very common way to say 'need to': the verb gerekmek (to be necessary) paired with a nominalized (infinitive) form of the main verb carrying a possessive suffix that marks WHO needs to do it -- git-me-m gerekiyor (literally 'my going is necessary' = I need to go). Crucially, 'gerekiyor' itself never changes person -- it's always 3rd person singular, because grammatically the thing that IS necessary is 'my going', not 'I'.
b1-gerekmek.fact: -mAlI expresses the speaker's own judgment ('su içmeliyim' = I must drink water, I've decided), while gerekmek reads as more neutral/external necessity ('su içmem gerekiyor' = drinking water is something I need) -- in everyday speech Turks use them close to interchangeably, but gerekmek is often preferred for more objective, fact-based necessity.

dialogue.tr: Neden bu kadar erken gitmen gerekiyor?
dialogue.en: Why do you need to leave so early?
I have an important meeting tomorrow.

b1-aorist.title: Aorist (-Ir): General Truths and Habits
b1-aorist.pattern: stem + -Ir (harmonized: ır/ir/ur/ür, or bare -r after a vowel-final stem)
b1-aorist.explanation: The aorist expresses general truths, habits, and characteristic behavior -- 'su 100 derecede kaynar' (water boils at 100 degrees), not a specific ongoing action. Vowel-final stems just add bare -r (izle-r, I watch/he watches). Polysyllabic consonant-final stems reliably follow 4-way harmony (değiştir-ir, çalış-ır). A handful of very common MONOSYLLABIC consonant-final verbs are genuine, specific exceptions to that harmony: gitmek->gider, etmek->eder, yapmak->yapar, bakmak->bakar, kanmak->kanar all take -Ar/-Er instead of the harmony-predicted -Ir/-Ir.
b1-aorist.fact: Despite a popular belief that 'monosyllabic verbs are always irregular,' most aren't -- almak (alır), bilmek (bilir), bulmak (bulur), durmak (durur), gelmek (gelir), görmek (görür), kalmak (kalır), olmak (olur), ölmek (ölür), varmak (varır), vermek (verir), vurmak (vurur), and sanmak (sanır) all follow the regular 4-way pattern perfectly. It's specifically gitmek/etmek/yapmak/bakmak/kanmak that don't.
